Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure, helping to alert you to possible high blood pressure issues. However, these devices do not provide actual blood pressure readings.

Some smart rings and other fitness devices also have this capability, but they require periodic calibration with a traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to provide full blood pressure measurements without any calibration, citing clinical trials involving thousands of people in support of this claim...

"Silent killer"

Abnormally high blood pressure (hypertension) and abnormally low blood pressure (hypotension) can both pose significant health risks.

Of the two, high blood pressure is more dangerous and is often referred to as the "silent killer" because it can cause serious and irreversible damage to the arteries, heart, and brain without any obvious symptoms. Many cases are only discovered after triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Older adults in particular should monitor their blood pressure regularly. There are also various home upper-arm blood pressure monitors available on the market for convenient self-measurement. However, it would naturally be more ideal if the fitness device you wear could monitor blood pressure fully automatically.

Apple Watch blood pressure feature

With the launch of watchOS 26, five Apple Watch models will be able to measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these devices will not provide any readings; they will only alert you when signs of possible high blood pressure are detected. Other devices such as the Oura Ring operate in a similar manner.

Some fitness devices can indeed provide actual blood pressure readings, but they require regular calibration with readings from a blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup Vital Signals says it has developed a smart ring called the Signal Ring that can measure blood pressure without any calibration, with accuracy comparable to traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitors.

According to Bloomberg, CEO Tom Moss said he had nearly died from undiagnosed high blood pressure, which was precisely the reason he founded the company.

The ring will begin accepting pre-orders later today, ship in October, and is priced at US$399 with no subscription required. The accompanying app (see image above) can display real-time blood pressure readings and long-term blood pressure trends.

It is worth noting that the Oura Ring has not yet received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but clinical trials have shown that the device can provide accurate blood pressure readings for thousands of participants.

Interestingly, Moss has no intention of selling this ring to everyone. He said these professional features are best suited for older adults and those assessed by doctors as being at risk of high blood pressure, meaning the Signal Ring's performance in other areas (such as sleep tracking) is relatively average.
